data.answer:
**Large businesses are much more likely to own IP rights, and to combine different types of rights.** The 2020 research paper, using 2016–17 data, found that 43.9 per cent of large businesses owned patents, trade marks or designs, compared with 3.2 per cent of SMEs.[1]

- **SMEs’ portfolios are more concentrated in trade marks.** Among IP-owning businesses, 88.7 per cent of SMEs held trade marks only, compared with 73.6 per cent of large businesses. Large businesses more often combined patents and trade marks (11.2 versus 3.0 per cent) or held all three rights (8.4 versus 1.3 per cent).[2]
- **Resources help explain the difference.** The 2020 report notes that IP ownership involves attorney, application, renewal and sometimes litigation costs. Larger businesses tend to have greater financial, knowledge and organisational resources to apply for and use rights.[3]
- **SME use has nevertheless been growing.** The 2022 report recorded an increase in SMEs with an active right from 2 per cent in 2002 to 4 per cent in 2017, driven mainly by trade marks. The 2024 report found that, over the preceding two decades, the number of patent-holding SMEs had grown at five times the rate of SMEs overall—a pattern not observed for large firms.[4]
- **Patents can serve different commercialisation roles.** The 2024 report describes patents as helping small innovators trade technology with larger firms that have established commercialisation resources, while also giving small firms time to secure resources and finance.[5]

These differences do not mean IP use is confined to established businesses: the 2024 report still found large firms more likely to patent than smaller firms, but young firms aged 0–5 more likely to patent than older firms.[6]
